sections.content: St. Paul, Minnesota is one of the Midwest's most underrated real estate markets. While its twin city Minneapolis often grabs the headlines, St. Paul offers investors something arguably more valuable: lower entry prices, steady rental demand, and a growing population of motivated sellers. Whether you are a seasoned wholesaler, a first-time flipper, or a buy-and-hold landlord, there are real estate deals in St. Paul MN worth pursuing right now. If you are just getting started, check out our full Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide before diving in.
St. Paul MN Real Estate Market Overview

St. Paul is the state capital of Minnesota and home to roughly 310,000 residents. The city sits on the eastern bank of the Mississippi River and borders Minneapolis to the west. It has a diverse economy anchored by healthcare, education, government, and manufacturing — which means stable employment and consistent housing demand. The University of St. Thomas, Hamline University, and several large hospital systems all drive renter demand year-round.

As of 2024, the median home price in St. Paul sits around $260,000 to $280,000 — significantly below the national median and well below Minneapolis prices. That gap creates real opportunity for investors who can identify undervalued properties and act quickly. The city has seen modest appreciation of 4 to 6 percent annually over the past three years, which is healthy but not overheated. Inventory remains tight, which keeps rental vacancy rates low — typically between 3 and 5 percent citywide.
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in St. Paul

Not every zip code in St. Paul performs the same for investors. Knowing which neighborhoods align with your strategy — whether that is wholesaling, flipping, or renting — makes all the difference. Explore current deal activity across the city on our St. Paul MN market page.
Top Investor-Friendly Neighborhoods

items: Frogtown (Thomas-Dale): One of the most affordable neighborhoods in the city, with median prices often under $200,000. High density of older homes creates strong wholesale and flip opportunities. Strong rental demand from working-class families and students.

West Side: A culturally vibrant neighborhood with a mix of single-family homes and small multifamily properties. Growing interest from first-time buyers is pushing prices up, creating equity for early investors.
Payne-Phalen: Located on the East Side, this neighborhood offers entry-level prices and improving infrastructure. Investors are picking up duplexes and triplexes here at strong cap rates.
North End: One of the most active areas for distressed properties and motivated sellers. Homes here can be acquired well below ARV, making it a hotspot for wholesalers.
Dayton's Bluff: Perched on a bluff overlooking downtown, this area has historic homes with strong renovation upside. Flippers who can manage rehab costs find strong ARVs here.
Highland Park: A more established neighborhood with higher prices but strong rental demand near the river. Best for buy-and-hold investors targeting quality tenants and lower turnover.

sections.content: Drive the North End and Frogtown neighborhoods during the first two weeks of the month — that is when property owners who are behind on bills are most likely to respond to a direct mail campaign or door knock. Timing your outreach to financial pressure cycles increases your conversion rate significantly.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in St. Paul MN
Wholesale Deals

Wholesaling is active in St. Paul, particularly in distressed neighborhoods like North End, Frogtown, and Payne-Phalen. The key is finding motivated sellers — people facing foreclosure, probate situations, divorce, or deferred maintenance they cannot afford. Assignment fees in St. Paul typically range from $8,000 to $20,000 depending on the deal. To get started with the fundamentals, read our guide on Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners. St. Paul also has a solid network of cash buyers — local flippers and landlords who are actively looking for inventory.
Fix and Flip Deals

St. Paul is rich with older housing stock — many homes were built between 1900 and 1960, which means there is no shortage of properties needing updates. A typical flip in neighborhoods like Dayton's Bluff or West Side might involve purchasing a home for $160,000, putting $50,000 to $70,000 into renovation, and selling for $280,000 to $310,000. That leaves room for a solid profit margin after carrying costs and commissions. Use our free ARV Calculator to quickly estimate after-repair value before you make an offer.
Rental Properties

Buy-and-hold investing is one of the strongest strategies in St. Paul right now. Average rents for a two-bedroom unit range from $1,200 to $1,600 per month, while three-bedroom single-family homes rent for $1,500 to $2,100. With purchase prices still in the $200,000 to $260,000 range in many neighborhoods, investors can achieve positive cash flow with a standard 20 to 25 percent down payment. Multifamily properties — duplexes and triplexes — are especially attractive and can be found in Payne-Phalen and the East Side for under $350,000.
How to Find Off-Market Deals in St. Paul

The most profitable deals rarely show up on the MLS. To consistently find real estate deals in St. Paul MN at below-market prices, you need to build off-market pipelines. Our detailed guide on How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals covers the full playbook, but here are the most effective tactics for the St. Paul market specifically.

items: Direct mail to absentee owners and tax-delinquent properties in Ramsey County — the county assessor's database is publicly accessible and updated regularly.
Driving for dollars in Frogtown and North End, looking for signs of deferred maintenance: overgrown yards, boarded windows, tarped roofs.
Probate leads from the Ramsey County probate court — estates with real property often need to sell quickly and below market.
Building relationships with local attorneys who handle estate planning, divorce, and bankruptcy — they refer clients who need fast property sales.
Connecting with local wholesalers at the Minnesota Real Estate Investors Association (MnREIA) monthly meetups in the Twin Cities metro.
Using AI-powered platforms to automate lead generation and identify motivated sellers before they hit the market.

sections.content: St. Paul Real Estate Market Trends to Watch in 2024

Several trends are shaping the investment landscape in St. Paul right now. First, the city has been investing heavily in infrastructure along the Green Line light rail corridor, which runs from downtown St. Paul to Minneapolis. Properties within a half mile of light rail stops have seen above-average appreciation and are attracting new development. Second, rising interest rates have pushed some would-be buyers back into the rental market, which is a net positive for landlords. Third, St. Paul's rent control ordinance — which caps rent increases at 3 percent per year for most properties — is something every investor must understand before buying. The ordinance applies to most residential rental units, so run your numbers accordingly.

The investors who win in St. Paul are the ones who understand the neighborhoods block by block — not just the city as a whole. Local knowledge and fast analysis are what separate profitable deals from expensive mistakes.
Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting St. Paul MN

St. Paul is an attractive target for out-of-state investors, especially those coming from high-cost markets like California, New York, or Seattle. The price-to-rent ratios are more favorable, and the market is less competitive than coastal cities. However, investing remotely requires a different approach. Before you run the numbers on any deal, make sure you know how to analyze real estate deals like a pro so you avoid overpaying or underestimating renovation costs.

items: Build your local team first: Find a St. Paul-based property manager, a contractor who knows local building codes, and a real estate attorney familiar with Minnesota landlord-tenant law before you buy.

Understand Minnesota's cold weather impact on rehab costs: Properties here need winterization, updated HVAC systems, and insulated pipes — budget an extra 10 to 15 percent for climate-related repairs compared to warmer markets.
Research Ramsey County property taxes carefully — they can run $3,000 to $6,000 annually on investment properties and significantly affect your cash flow projections.
Use our free Wholesale Deal Calculator to model your maximum allowable offer before you submit anything on a St. Paul property.
Visit the market at least once before buying — walk the neighborhoods, meet your property manager in person, and inspect comparable properties so your underwriting reflects reality.
Account for St. Paul's rent control ordinance in your long-term cash flow projections — assume rent growth of no more than 3 percent per year for budgeting purposes.

sections.content: When analyzing St. Paul rental properties, use a vacancy rate of 6 to 8 percent in your projections even though current vacancy is lower. Markets shift, and building in that buffer ensures your deal still works if conditions soften. Conservative underwriting is what keeps investors in the game long-term.
Is St. Paul a Good Market for Real Estate Investors Right Now?

The short answer is yes — but with eyes open. St. Paul offers affordable entry prices, strong rental demand, a steady supply of distressed properties, and a metro economy that is resilient across cycles. The rent control ordinance adds a layer of complexity, but investors who factor it into their analysis can still build strong portfolios here. The key is finding deals below market value, managing your rehab costs tightly, and building a local team you can trust. Those three things will determine whether St. Paul becomes a profitable market for you or an expensive lesson.
